overview.title: Developer overview
overview.lead: Bibi has four ways in: the web app, a REST API, a GraphQL graph and an MCP server. They all run the same operations with the same permissions.
overview.body:
# One set of operations, four surfaces

Every capability in Bibi is defined once as a **core operation**, for example `venue.create` or `order.list`. Each operation has an input schema, an output schema, a required permission and a handler. The surfaces are generated from that list:

- **REST** at `{{webUrl}}/api/v1`, described by an OpenAPI 3.1 document.
- **GraphQL** at `{{webUrl}}/api/graphql`, for reading related data in one request.
- **MCP** at `{{mcpUrl}}/mcp`, one tool per operation, for AI assistants such as Claude.
- **The web app**, which staff use every day.

Because everything comes from the same operations, a command that exists in the web app also exists in REST and MCP, with the same validation and the same errors. A parity test in CI keeps it that way.

# Tenancy

All data belongs to an **organization**. Every credential resolves to one user in one organization, and every operation is scoped to that organization. You can never read or change another organization's data, whichever surface you use.

# Audit and logging

Every command writes an audit log entry with the actor (`user` or `ai`), the surface and a request id. Organization admins can read the history in the app and through `auditLog.list`.

# Where to go next

- [Authentication](/developers/authentication): API keys, sessions and OAuth.
- [REST API](/developers/rest-api) and the [REST reference]({{webUrl}}/api/v1/docs).
- [MCP server](/developers/mcp) and the [MCP tool reference](/developers/reference/mcp).
- [AI approvals](/developers/approvals): why AI commands become proposals.
- [Errors and limits](/developers/errors).

authentication.title: Authentication
authentication.lead: Every request is made as a user in one organization. Use an API key for server-to-server integrations and OAuth for MCP clients and third-party apps.
authentication.body:
# API keys (REST and GraphQL)

An API key belongs to the organization, not to a person. It has a preset (member, manager or admin), which an admin can fine-tune on the key's **Permissions** page. Send it as a bearer token:

```
Authorization: Bearer bib_<your key>
```

The `x-api-key: bib_<your key>` header works too. Keys always start with `bib_`.

- Keys are rate limited to 600 requests per minute.
- The key keeps working when the admin who created it leaves. Revoke it in **Settings** when it is no longer needed.
- Treat a key like a password. Never put it in front-end code or a public repository.

Only admins create, change and revoke API keys, under **Settings, Integrations**.

# OAuth 2.1 (MCP clients and apps)

MCP clients such as Claude Desktop sign in with OAuth. The client is sent to the Bibi sign-in page, the user signs in and picks an organization, and the client receives an access token that acts as that user.

- Discovery: `{{webUrl}}/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server`
- Protected resource metadata for MCP: `{{mcpUrl}}/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource`
- Authorization endpoint: `{{webUrl}}/api/auth/oauth2/authorize`
- Token endpoint: `{{webUrl}}/api/auth/oauth2/token`
- Scopes: `bibi:read` and `bibi:write`

Most MCP clients do all of this for you when you add the server URL.

# Session cookie

The web app uses a session cookie. Requests from a signed-in browser to `/api/v1` and `/api/graphql` are authenticated the same way. This is meant for the app itself, not for integrations.

# Permissions

Each member has one of three fixed roles: **member**, **manager** or **admin**. Every operation names the permission it needs, for example `venue:create`. The reference lists the permission for each route and tool. A call without it fails with `FORBIDDEN`.

rest-api.title: REST API
rest-api.lead: A JSON API under /api/v1 with one route per operation, described by an OpenAPI 3.1 document that is generated from the code.
rest-api.body:
# Base URL and spec

- Base URL: `{{webUrl}}/api/v1`
- OpenAPI document: [{{webUrl}}/api/v1/openapi.json]({{webUrl}}/api/v1/openapi.json)
- Interactive reference (browse every route and try requests): [{{webUrl}}/api/v1/docs]({{webUrl}}/api/v1/docs)

You can generate a typed client from the OpenAPI document with any OpenAPI generator.

# Requests

- Reads use `GET`. Query parameters carry filters and pagination.
- Creates use `POST`, updates use `PATCH`, archives and removals use `DELETE` or a `POST` to an action route.
- Bodies are JSON. Send `Content-Type: application/json`.
- Dates and times are ISO 8601 strings in UTC, for example `2026-11-05T09:00:00.000Z`.

```
curl "{{webUrl}}/api/v1/venues?limit=20" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer bib_<your key>"
```

# Pagination

List routes take `limit` (1 to 100, default 50) and `cursor`. The response has `items` and `nextCursor`. Pass `nextCursor` as `cursor` to get the next page. When `nextCursor` is `null` you have reached the end.

```
{ "items": [ ... ], "nextCursor": "clx2..." }
```

# Configurable fields

Organizations define their own types, fields and lists. Entities that support it carry a `fields` object with the organization's custom values. Read the organization's field definitions (`GET /field-definitions`) to know which keys and value types to expect. Item types can sit in the organization's own groups (`GET /item-type-groups`); a type's `groupId` names its group, and `GET /items?groupId=...` lists the items of one group.

# Responses and errors

Success returns `200` (or `201` for creates) with the operation's output as JSON. Failures return the error envelope described in [Errors and limits](/developers/errors).

# Payments, refunds and credit notes

Money moves at the organization's payment provider (Stripe, Swish) or accounting system, never in Bibi itself. A command writes its record first and then calls the provider, so the provider's result arrives a moment later:

- `POST /payments/{id}/refunds` (`payment.refund`): refund a paid payment in full or in part. The refund is `PENDING` until the provider confirms it. Needs `payment:refund`.
- `POST /payments/{id}/cancel` (`payment.cancel`): cancel a payment the customer has not paid yet.
- `POST /payments/manual` (`payment.recordManual`): record money received outside a provider, such as a bank transfer, against a quote, deposit request or invoice.
- `POST /invoices/{invoiceId}/credit-notes` (`invoice.credit`): credit a sent invoice in full, by line or by amount.

Read the result with `GET /payments/{id}` or `GET /invoices/{id}`. Credit notes are read with `GET /credit-notes?invoiceId=...` or `?orderId=...` (`creditNote.list`, paginated) and `GET /credit-notes/{id}` (`creditNote.get`), both with their credited lines; GraphQL has `creditNotes` and `creditNote`, MCP `creditNote_list` and `creditNote_get`. Needs `payment:read`.

A refund the provider does not confirm within 15 minutes is checked again at the provider every 15 minutes, and sent again under the same key if it never arrived there.

# Order versions

Bibi saves a version of an order's lines and headcount after every change (`orderVersion.list`, `GET /orders/{orderId}/versions`). Each version says whether it equals the order now (`isCurrent`), how many changes the order has against it, and which quotes were sent as it. A sent quote carries its `versionId`.

- `GET /order-versions/{id}` (`orderVersion.get`): the version's lines and what the order has changed since.
- `PUT /order-versions/{id}/name` (`orderVersion.name`): name a version, or send `null` to remove the name.
- `POST /order-versions/{id}/restore` (`orderVersion.restore`): set the order back to the version. The result is saved as a new version. Needs `program:write`.

A quote replaced by a newer one is `SUPERSEDED`. Accepting it (`quote.accept`) restores the order to that quote's version and declines the newer quote. `POST /quotes/{id}/reopen` (`quote.reopen`) sets it as the current version instead, without accepting: it is `SENT` again, the newer quote becomes `SUPERSEDED` and the order is restored to its version.

# Tasks

A task is a site visit, a tasting, a deadline or a note, of one of the organization's own task types (`GET /entity-types?base=TASK`). Only the type (`entityTypeId`) is required. A task can exist before any order and with no customer.

- Optional: `customerId`, `contactId` (needs a customer, and must work at it), `orderId` (needs a customer, and must be one of that customer's orders), `dueAt`, `assigneeId`, `note`, `fields` and `items`.
- `dueAt` is one instant, never a span. A task without one is not on the calendar or in Needs you, is never `overdue` and sorts last. `from` and `to` filter on it, so tasks without a due time appear only when neither is given.
- `items` lists the rooms the task concerns, each once: `{ itemId, hold, startsAt, endsAt }` with `hold` one of `RELATED`, `PREBOOK` or `BOOK`. Only active items of a bookable type are accepted, and a task takes no quantities. `RELATED` only names the room and takes no window. `PREBOOK` (a soft hold, may overlap) and `BOOK` (a hard hold that blocks) need their own `startsAt` before `endsAt`, unrelated to `dueAt`. Reading and changing rooms needs `item:read`.

- `GET /tasks` (`task.list`): filter by `customerId`, `orderId`, `assigneeId`, `statusId`, `state` (`open`, `done`, `overdue`) and `from`/`to`. Also `GET /customers/{customerId}/tasks` and `GET /orders/{orderId}/tasks`.
- `GET /tasks/{id}` (`task.get`): the task with `overdue`, its `statusId` and its `items`.
- `POST /tasks` (`task.create`): create a task. `orderId` links an order of the same customer right away; the assignee defaults to you (`assigneeId: null` leaves it unassigned).
- `PATCH /tasks/{id}` (`task.update`): change the type, customer, contact, order (`orderId`, `null` unlinks), `dueAt` (`null` clears it), `items`, note, fields or `assigneeId`. `items` replaces the rooms as a set (omitted keeps them, `[]` removes them all); a room kept keeps its id. `customerId: null` clears the customer, and then `contactId` and `orderId` must be `null` too. The order must belong to the task's customer, so moving to another customer needs a contact there (or `null`) and `orderId` `null` or one of its orders. The new assignee is notified.
- `POST /tasks/{id}/complete` and `POST /tasks/{id}/reopen` (`task.complete`, `task.reopen`): mark it done or open again. Done releases the holds for good: each `PREBOOK` and `BOOK` becomes `RELATED` without a window, and reopening does not hold anything again.
- `POST /tasks/{taskId}/order` (`task.linkOrder`): link the first order of the same customer. A task that is already linked returns `CONFLICT`; change it with `PATCH /tasks/{id}`.
- `POST /tasks/{id}/move` (`task.move`, body `{ statusId }`): move a task without an order to another pipeline status, like an order. See below.
- `DELETE /tasks/{id}` (`task.archive`): archive it. Archiving releases the holds; restoring holds them again.

A `PREBOOK` or `BOOK` holds its room for its own window while the task is open and not archived, like any other hold: it shows in availability and on the calendar with its `taskId`. A `BOOK` that collides with a hard hold, buffer or block returns `CONFLICT` with the issue path `items.<index>`, and nothing is saved. A window that is missing or ends before it starts, a room listed twice or an item that cannot be booked returns `VALIDATION` at `items.<index>`. `order.create` with `taskIds` carries each `PREBOOK` and `BOOK` over: it becomes a line of the new order for that item and window, in the item type's first soft-hold or hard-hold state (set by hand, so status moves keep it), and the task's room becomes `RELATED` in the same step, so the room is never held twice. A room one of the given `lines` already takes is not added again. An item type without such a state returns `VALIDATION` at `taskIds.<index>`; carrying rooms over needs `program:write`.

A task without an order sits in a pipeline status (`statusId`), one of the statuses flagged `tasks` (`orderStatus.create` and `orderStatus.update` take `tasks`, readable on `GET /order-statuses`; a closing status cannot have it, `VALIDATION` at `tasks` or `closes`). A new task takes the entry status if it holds tasks, else the first that does; with none flagged `statusId` is `null` and the task is on no board. Linking an order clears `statusId`, unlinking sets it again. Clearing the flag or archiving the status moves its tasks to the default status. `GET /tasks?statusId=` lists the tasks in a status.

`POST /tasks/{id}/move` accepts only a status that holds tasks (`VALIDATION` at `statusId`). A status that restricts its next moves allows only its listed targets, and of the gates into the target only `ASSIGNEE` applies (the task needs an assignee); `REASON` and `ACCEPTED_QUOTE` are skipped. A refused move changes nothing and returns `CONFLICT` with every blocker in `issues`, with the path `id` (the task has an order or is done), `statusId` (not allowed from its status) or `assigneeId`. An open task without an order is a card on the board: `GET /pipeline` returns them in `taskCards` (`id`, `columnId`, `statusId`, `typeName`, `customerId`, `dueAt`, `overdue`, `assigneeId`, `allowedStatusIds`), empty without `task:read` or with an order type filter.

Reads need `task:read`, changes `task:write` and archiving `task:delete`. An open task with a due time that is today or overdue shows in its assignee's Needs you with the key `TASK_DUE:<taskId>`.

graphql.title: GraphQL
graphql.lead: A read-focused graph for fetching related data in one request, for example an order with its program, requirements and run sheets.
graphql.body:
# Endpoint

`POST {{webUrl}}/api/graphql` with a JSON body of `query`, `variables` and optionally `operationName`. Authenticate the same way as REST (API key, OAuth token or session).

```
curl -X POST "{{webUrl}}/api/graphql" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer bib_<your key>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"query":"{ venues { items { id name } } }"}'
```

# Schema

The schema is generated from the same operations and Zod schemas as REST and MCP. Every entity can be read through the graph, and every command is also available as a mutation.

Introspection is turned off in production. Get the schema as SDL from the MCP tool `graphql_schema`, or run the app locally where GraphiQL and introspection are on.

# Limits

Queries are checked for depth and cost before they run. A query that is too deep or too expensive is rejected with a validation error. Split it into smaller queries or use pagination.

# When to use GraphQL or REST

- Use **GraphQL** to read a tree of related data in one round trip.
- Use **REST** for simple integrations, webhooks-style syncs and anything where an OpenAPI client is convenient.

mcp.title: MCP server
mcp.lead: Connect Claude or any other MCP client to Bibi. The assistant works as you, with your permissions, and every change waits for your approval.
mcp.body:
# Server URL

`{{mcpUrl}}/mcp` (Streamable HTTP). The server is stateless: each request is authenticated with an OAuth access token.

# Connect a client

1. In your MCP client (for example Claude Desktop or Claude Code), add a remote MCP server with the URL above.
2. The client opens the Bibi sign-in page. Sign in and choose the organization.
3. The client receives a token and lists the tools. You are ready.

The client discovers the authorization server through `{{mcpUrl}}/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource`, so there is nothing else to configure.

# Tools

There is one tool per core operation. The name is the operation name with dots replaced by underscores: `venue.create` becomes `venue_create`. Each tool has a JSON Schema for its input and output, and hints that tell the client whether it is read-only or changes data. See the full [MCP tool reference](/developers/reference/mcp).

Two generic tools make reading easier:

- `graphql_schema` returns the GraphQL schema as SDL.
- `graphql_query` runs a read-only GraphQL query. Mutations are rejected.

The assistant also gets the organization's own field and type names in the tool descriptions, so it can use the words your venue uses.

# Changes need approval

When an AI assistant calls a tool that changes data, Bibi does **not** run it. It answers with `status: approval_required` and a short summary. The user approves or cancels the proposal in the Bibi app. Read [AI approvals](/developers/approvals) for the details.

# Untrusted content

Some tools return text that came from outside the organization, for example received e-mails. These tools are marked as untrusted output, so clients and the assistant treat the content as data, never as instructions.

approvals.title: AI approvals
approvals.lead: AI proposes, people decide. Commands called by an AI actor are turned into proposals that a person must approve in the app.
approvals.body:
# How it works

1. The assistant calls a command, for example `order_create`.
2. Instead of running it, the MCP server returns a proposal:

```
{
  "status": "approval_required",
  "operation": "order.create",
  "summary": "Create order Board meeting on 5 Nov for Acme AB",
  "approvalToken": "...",
  "expiresAt": "2026-11-04T10:10:00.000Z"
}
```

3. The app shows the proposal as a card. The user reads the summary and clicks **Approve** or **Cancel**.
4. On approval, the app runs the command as the user. The audit log records `actor=ai`, the conversation and who approved it.

Proposals expire after 10 minutes. The assistant must not retry a command that is waiting for approval.

# What needs approval

- Every command (anything that changes data) called by an AI actor needs approval by default.
- Queries (reads) never need approval.
- The reference marks each route and tool that needs approval with a badge.

# Integrations with API keys

Calls made with an API key or by a person in the app are not AI calls. They run directly, with the permissions of the key or the user. Approval is only for AI actors.

errors.title: Errors and limits
errors.lead: Every surface returns the same typed errors, with a stable code, a message and field-level issues.
errors.body:
# Error envelope

REST returns errors as JSON with a matching HTTP status:

```
{
  "error": {
    "code": "VALIDATION",
    "message": "Invalid input",
    "issues": [ { "path": "name", "message": "Required" } ]
  }
}
```

`issues[].path` is the field, dot-joined for nested fields (`rooms.0.name`). MCP tools return the same object with `isError: true`. GraphQL puts the code in `errors[].extensions.code`.

# Codes

- `VALIDATION` (400): the input did not match the schema. Check `issues`.
- `UNAUTHENTICATED` (401): no credential or an invalid one.
- `FORBIDDEN` (403): signed in, but the role lacks the permission or you are not a member of the organization.
- `NOT_FOUND` (404): the record does not exist in your organization.
- `CONFLICT` (409): the change clashes with existing data, for example an overlapping occupancy or a duplicate name.
- `UNAVAILABLE` (503): a capability is not set up right now, for example no AI model is configured.
- `INTERNAL` (500): something went wrong on our side. Retry later and quote the request id if you contact support.

# Limits

- API keys: 600 requests per minute.
- List pages: at most 100 items per request.
- GraphQL: queries have a maximum depth and cost.
- MCP `graphql_query`: queries only, with a maximum length.

# Retries

Reads are safe to retry. For commands, check the result before retrying a request that timed out, so you do not create the same record twice.
